Introduction In the contemporary epoch, the exploitation of the world's oceans and seas is undergoing rapid expansion, with the ocean economy demonstrating consistent growth and assuming an increasingly pivotal role in the national economies of all nations worldwide. Indeed, more than 80 % of global trade is dependent on maritime transport, with global maritime trade growing by 2.4 % in 2023, reversing the contraction in 2022 to 12.3 billion tons (UNCTAD, 2024). Despite this, the Safety and Shipping Report 2022, published by Allianz, states that the global shipping industry still faces a series of challenges, including geopolitical events, wars, piracy and climate change (Allianz, 2022). Safety is recognized as a perpetual concern for the advancement of the shipping industry. The occurrence of major maritime emergencies has led to a deterioration in the global maritime security landscape. The loss of human life and property in the event of a major maritime emergency is a significant concern, and the pollution caused by the accident will also have a devastating effect on marine biodiversity and ecological balance. The implementation of effective emergency management in the aftermath of major emergencies is therefore crucial to minimize losses and impacts. Against the background of continuous development and change in the country, society and industry, organizational structures have become more complex, internal elements more diverse and the external environment more variable. Clarifying the internal logic between maritime safety management(MSM) and maritime emergency management(MEM) can help realize the synergistic development of maritime safety and emergency response. MSM focuses on the prevention and control of maritime accidents, while MEM focuses on the response and disposal of maritime emergencies. MSM and MEM are interrelated, intertwined and mutually supportive. Together, they build a comprehensive maritime safety and security system. The primary causative factors for maritime accidents are commonly ascribed to human error, technical failures, and mechanical faults (Celik and Cebi, 2009). Nonetheless, in the occurrence of a maritime emergency, the absence of proactive and effective measures for MEM will precipitate further losses with regard to human life, property, and the marine environment. The International Maritime Organization (IMO) has developed a number of pertinent conventions, including International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), International Convention on Maritime Search and Rescue (SAR), International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification, and Watchkeeping for Seafarers (STCW), International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), and International Convention on Oil Pollution Preparedness, Response and Cooperation (OPRC), with the purpose of addressing this challenge. These conventions stipulate the requirement for ships to possess contingency plans for a range of potential maritime emergencies, such as fire, collision, and grounding. Furthermore, they call for regular drills to ensure that the crew is well-acquainted with emergency response procedures, thereby enhancing the ship's overall crisis management capabilities (IMO, 2024). The IMO has outlined the SAR responsibilities of each contracting state and has stipulated that states must establish effective maritime SAR services (IMO, 2006). Furthermore, the IMO has mandated that seafarers must receive emergency response training, encompassing, inter alia, training in firefighting, lifesaving, first aid, and pollution prevention (IMO, 2018). Ships must possess a Shipboard Oil Pollution Emergency Plan (SOPEP) and, in the case of ships transporting toxic liquid substances, a Sea Pollution Contingency Plan for Toxic Liquid Substances (SMPEP) (IMO, 2005). In addition, states parties are obligated to establish national oil pollution preparedness and response systems, including the establishment of oil pollution emergency command centers, the stockpiling of emergency equipment and materials, and the training of emergency personnel (IMO, 1995). The issuance of these treaties aims to promote the strengthening of international cooperation in the emergency management for maritime emergencies, and enhance the coordinated response capabilities of all nations, thereby promoting sustainable and healthy development of the global shipping industry. It is evident that the majority of scholars concentrate on research pertaining to the identification, assessment and control of safety risks for maritime accidents, with these research endeavors effectively promoting the enhancement for global maritime transport safety management to a certain extent. However, some scholars have undertaken reviews of the research outcomes pertaining to maritime accidents, encompassing various topics across distinct time periods, as shown in Table 1. As shown in Table 1, the themes of existing maritime transport safety reviews primarily encompass risk analysis and assessment for maritime transport accidents, maritime transport safety management, and maritime transport resilience. However, there is limited attention devoted to emergency management issues under maritime transport emergencies. In this study, we focus on MEM in the context of emergencies. In addressing the challenges faced by current MEM, as well as the existing ambiguity surrounding the research themes, this study aims to systematically address the research related to MEM through various approaches. This will assist in clarifying the development lineage, thematic evolution, research focal points and developmental trends in MEM research, and furnish novel perspectives and concepts for future research in this domain. fetched_contents.text: A Bibliometric Analysis of Child Language During 1900–2021 Abstract This study purposed to provide a bibliometric overview of child language (CL) research from 1900 to 2021 and identify major trends in CL. A total of 48,453 research articles related to the CL were identified from the Web of Science. Co-authorship, co-word, and co-citation analysis was conducted by using VOSviewer and CiteSpace. The following was analyzed: annual distribution of related papers; related disciplines; mainstream journals; geographical and institutional distribution; hot topics; keyword burst detection; and co-citation analysis of journals, authors, and references. Results showed that, under the impact of new empirical methods and new theories, the field of CL is undergoing great changes. Research hotspot and the research trends mainly concentrated on autism spectrum disorder, school readiness, oral language, reading comprehension, exposure, bilingualism, vocabulary, input, skills, kindergarten, cochlear implants, and intervention. More and more pieces of research focus on the individual difference in CL development and the importance of intervention in language education by typically developing children and some children with disabilities or language disorders. Besides, child second language acquisition also attracted a lot of attention. This bibliometric analysis is of great reference significance for researchers to understand the progress and discipline development trend in this field. Keywords: child language, bibliometric analysis, VOSviewer, CiteSpace, visualization Introduction Language learning and development in early childhood is the most critical period of one’s life. The excellent way of child language (CL) acquisition has long attracted the attention of researchers. As early as the 18th century, German Philosopher Dietrich Tiedemann observed and described the psychological and linguistic development process of his child. The early research on children’s language acquisition mainly adopted the method of diary recording (e.g., Donahue, 1993). Since the 1960s, foreign psychologists and linguists have adopted empirical research methods and conducted many detailed studies on children’s language acquisition. In the past 30 years, some nativists represented by Norm Chomsky have focused on the study of principle and parameter theory. fetched_contents.text: Visibility, impact, and applications of bibliometric software tools through citation analysis Abstract This study examines the visibility, impact, and applications of bibliometric software tools in the peer-reviewed literature through a “Cited Reference Search” using the Web of Science (WOS) database. A total of 2882 citing research articles to eight bibliometric software tools were extracted from the WOS Core Collection between 2010 and 2021. These citing articles are analyzed by publication year, country, publication title, publisher, open access level, funding agency, and WOS category. Mentions of bibliometric software tools in Author Keywords and KeyWords Plus are also compared. The VOSviewer software is utilized to identify specific research areas by discipline from the keyword co-occurrences of the citing articles. The findings reveal that while bibliometric software tools are making a noteworthy impact and contribution to research, their visibility through referencing, Author Keywords, and KeyWords Plus is limited. This study serves as a clarion call to raise awareness and initiate discussions on the citing practices of software tools in scholarly publications. Keywords: Bibliometric software, Citation analysis, Scholarly publications, Author keywords, KeyWords plus, VOSviewer Introduction Software is a set of instructions or commands that tell a computer what to do (Bainbridge, 2004; Chun, 2005). Scientific software (i.e., non-trivial) is a complex software program with a broad range of functionality used for advanced tasks that require regular updates to fix bugs, improve performance, address security issues, and enhance compatibility (e.g., bibliometric software tools). On the other hand, non-scientific software (i.e., trivial) refers to basic software programs with minimal functionality designed for general tasks (e.g., unit converter). Nowadays, researchers are becoming more dependent on scientific software, particularly in the STEM fields. Content analysis studies on software in specific scientific journals confirm that software is significantly involved in research [e.g., PLOS ONE (Li et al., 2017; Pan et al., 2015, 2016), Nature (Nangia & Katz, 2017), and Science (Katz & Chue Hong, 2018)]. Software is thus a creative and critical aspect of research that merits recognition and credit. Despite its importance, scholarly publications have traditionally overlooked the citation of software, highlighting a need for increased awareness of its acknowledgement in the research process. The tendency to view software as a technical contribution rather than an original scholarly work may be a contributing factor to this lack of recognition (Soito & Hwang, 2016). Moreover, the changing nature of software over time with authorship, roles, and credits presents its own issues with accurately citing and referencing. According to Alliez et al. (2020), “First, software authorship is extremely varied, involving many roles: software architect, coder, debugger, tester, team manager, and so on. Second, software itself is a complex object: the lifespan can range from a few months to decades, the size can range to a few dozens of lines of code to several millions, and it can be stand-alone or rely on multiple external packages. And finally, sometimes one may want to reference a particular version of a given software (this is crucial for reproducible research), while at other times one may want to cite the software as a whole” (pp. 1–2). Bouquin et al. (2020) point out, “It is also important to recognize that software citation standards are still being normalized in all disciplines, and software developed for one discipline may be used in entirely different contexts.” Further, studies reveal that LIS scholars tend to cite a related publication compared to biologists who cite software directly (Pan et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2018). Citation of software poses challenges not only from its recognition and standardization but also from the academic culture and disciplinary norms (Katz & Chue Hong, 2018). However, such academic hurdles can be mitigated by working with diverse communities, including researchers, librarians, indexers, publishers, professional societies, editors, reviewers, archivists, funders, and other stakeholders, to bring educational awareness and facilitate necessary changes for proper software citation practices (Katz et al., 2019a, 2019b; Niemeyer et al., 2016). Bibliometric software tools are one type of non-trivial software designed to assist scientific tasks that are considered essential for conducting bibliometric and scientometric analyses in research (Bales et al., 2020; Bankar & Lihitkar, 2019; Cobo et al., 2011; Moral-Muñoz et al., 2020; Pradhan, 2016; van Eck & Waltman, 2014). The emergence of sophisticated software tools has revolutionized how data is analyzed, visualized, and differentiated. Consequently, this has enabled researchers to capture, refine, and analyze large data sets that would have been otherwise impossible to process. To this end, the present study examines the visibility, impact, and applications of bibliometric software tools within scholarly articles, thereby highlighting their pivotal significance in academic research. Bibliometric methods are used to evaluate research impact by combining quantitative indicators with network-based analysis of scholarly relationships. The most commonly used indicators are citations and co-citations, which measure influence and connectivity across the literature. Citation analysis assesses how often a work is referenced, often used as a proxy for scholarly importance and reach, while co-citation analysis identifies clusters of papers that are cited together, revealing conceptual proximity and shared intellectual foundations [N1-R1][N1-R5]. In research impact evaluation, these methods help distinguish highly influential papers from those with broader but less concentrated influence, and they can also highlight seminal or foundational works that shape later scholarship [N1-R2][N1-R5].

Citation analysis and co-citation analysis inform impact assessment by providing two complementary lenses. Citation counts and citation networks can identify papers or authors with high visibility and influence, while co-citation networks map thematic linkages and show which topics or schools of thought are central to the field [N1-R1][N1-R5]. Co-citation is especially useful for identifying emergent or evolving areas of research because it captures the literature that scholars simultaneously reference when discussing a topic, rather than only the direct citations of one paper [N1-R5]. This makes it a valuable tool for assessing not just popularity, but also conceptual significance and interdisciplinary reach [N1-R2].

Publication trends and author/institution networks reveal research prominence by showing where and how scholarship is concentrated over time. Network analysis examines relationships between publications, authors, or institutions, and can visualize how research activity is distributed across journals, regions, and organizations [N1-R4]. Trends in annual publication volume, journal clusters, institutional affiliations, and author collaboration patterns can indicate which institutions or countries are dominant in a field, which journals are most influential, and which subfields are growing rapidly [N1-R4]. These methods thus go beyond simple citation counts by exposing the structural and collaborative dynamics that underpin research prominence [N1-R4].

A major limitation is that these methods are not neutral. Citation bias can inflate the apparent impact of papers that are easier to cite, more recent, or appear in prestigious journals, while authorship bias can concentrate credit in a few prolific or highly connected individuals or institutions [N4-R1][N4-R3]. Interpretive ambiguity remains because citations do not always reflect the actual importance or quality of a paper, and bibliometric results can be shaped by how databases are searched, how records are selected, and how thresholds are set [N4-R2][N4-R4]. As a result, bibliometric impact assessment should be treated as a descriptive and exploratory tool, rather than a definitive measure of research value [N4-R2][N4-R4].

Methodological choices in bibliometric work typically center on data sources and databases, search strategies, and analytical tools. The most common databases are Web of Science, Scopus, and other large citation-indexed platforms, which provide the foundational records for citation counts, authorships, and publication metadata [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In practice, studies often combine these databases to maximize coverage, though the exact selection can affect validity because different databases capture different sets of journals and disciplines [N5-F4]. Tools such as VOSviewer and CiteSpace are widely used for network construction and visualization, while software like Bibliometrix and ScientoPy support more specialized scientometric analysis [N5-R1][N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. These tools help researchers transform raw bibliometric data into maps, co-occurrence networks, and citation burst analyses [N5-R1][N5-R4].

Search strategies and inclusion/exclusion criteria are central to validity because they define what counts as “research” and which records are included in the analysis. A narrow search may miss relevant papers, while a broad search may include irrelevant or low-quality records [N4-R2][N4-R3]. Criteria for inclusion often depend on the study’s purpose, such as whether to restrict to peer-reviewed articles, to limit to a specific time period, or to exclude conference proceedings or book chapters [N4-R2][N4-R3]. The choice of keywords, subject categories, and filtering rules also shapes the sample, so a search that misses key terms may fail to capture important subfields or recent trends [N4-R2][N4-R3]. Because bibliometric analysis is highly sensitive to these choices, replication and transparency are essential for validity [N4-R2][N4-R3].

Common limitations include citation bias, authorship bias, and interpretive ambiguity. Citation bias occurs when papers are cited not only because they are important, but because they are easier to cite, more recent, or appear in highly cited journals [N4-R1]. Authorship bias may arise when highly connected authors or institutions dominate the network, obscuring contributions from less visible actors [N4-R3]. Interpretive ambiguity exists because bibliometric outputs are often open to multiple readings: a high citation count may reflect popularity rather than quality, a dense network may signal collaboration rather than cohesion, and a burst of keywords may indicate emergence rather than significance [N4-R2][N4-R4]. Additionally, the field-specific use of software and databases can introduce bias if the tools used are not well suited to the research question or if they are limited by disciplinary citation norms [N5-F4]. Overall, these methodological choices and limitations mean that bibliometric findings should be interpreted cautiously and complemented by qualitative or theoretical analysis [N4-R2][N4-R4].

This indicates that policy is not treated as an external context, but as a central component of maritime safety and emergency management research [N2-F1][N2-F2].

The maritime emergency management evidence states that effective emergency management is crucial to minimize losses and impacts following major maritime emergencies, and that ships must possess contingency plans for potential emergencies such as fire, collision, and grounding [N2-F1]. It also notes that states parties must establish national oil pollution preparedness and response systems, including emergency command centers and training of emergency personnel [N2-F1]. The maritime transportation safety management review similarly emphasizes that effective emergency management is critical in cases of heavy casualties or large-scale oil spill pollution, and that search-and-rescue (SAR) requirements at sea also require effective emergency responses [N2-F2]. ## 5) Overall synthesis

In maritime safety and emergency management, bibliometric methods have been utilized to do more than simply count citations. They are used to evaluate **research impact** by combining citations, co-citations, and network analysis to assess influence, conceptual prominence, and structural collaboration [N1-R1][N1-R5][N1-R4]. They are used to identify **research trends and hotspots** through topic modeling, keyword co-occurrence, co-citation analysis, and burst detection, helping to locate emerging topics such as risk assessment, incident response, policy, and search-and-rescue [N2-R1][N2-R4][N3-R2][N3-F3][N3-R4]. They are also used to reveal **methodological choices and limitations**, including database selection, search strategy sensitivity, citation bias, authorship bias, and interpretive ambiguity [N1-R1][N5-F4][N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R4].

What makes maritime bibliometrics especially meaningful is that they are embedded in a field with strong practical and policy dimensions. The evidence shows that maritime research is shaped by real-world risks, institutional frameworks, and operational constraints, and that policy, risk assessment, incident response, and search-and-rescue are not just abstract categories but central concerns in the literature [N2-F1][N2-F2]. At the same time, the methods are not perfect: they depend on the tools, databases, and criteria chosen, and their results should be interpreted carefully alongside qualitative and theoretical analysis [N5-F4][N4-R2][N4-R4].

In short, bibliometric methods in maritime safety and emergency management are best understood as a **descriptive and exploratory toolkit**. They help researchers evaluate impact, trace trends, and identify clusters, but they should be used with awareness of their limitations and with attention to the field-specific context in which maritime safety and emergency management are practiced and studied [N1-R1][N1-R2][N2-F1][N2-F2].
